sources.title: AI startups feared Nvidia’s money would dry up without Jensen Huang. His return as CEO has put those fears to rest
sources.text: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after just shy of two weeks of turmoil. The news—which has come as a shock to many in the tech world—was a welcome relief to investors and Nvidia’s partners, who had spent the majority of that time fretting that the company’s financial commitments might dry up. Nvidia has become what some have referred to as the “central bank of AI.” The company has invested in and supplied compute to various AI startups, neoclouds, and AI labs. These companies then, in part, use that money to buy Nvidia chips. Critics have called this process “circular financing,” with many saying it leaves much of the AI boom dangerously exposed to weak links. Indeed as of the end of July, Nvidia had invested nearly $50 billion in AI model makers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, and its equity stakes across the AI ecosystem totaled twice that. It has also pledged $170 billion of its investment-grade credit to help AI companies and neoclouds get financing. Before news of Huang’s reinstatement broke on Monday, several investors and Nvidia partners told Fortune they were concerned that these commitments might stall under the interim CEO. That interim CEO, Colette Kress, some said, already showed early signs of being more hesitant to make deals at the same rate as Huang. Any new CEO, they added, would likely want to appear as a steady hand and more cautious when it came to spending. “Jensen has been such a critical part of the ecosystem because he’s allowed Nvidia to provide compute to venture stage companies who otherwise don’t have access to it,” said one investor who asked to be anonymous to discuss private deals. “Everyone was concerned about whether the next person at the helm of Nvidia would also be as aggressive in fostering that ecosystem.” For a while, the investor said, any startup that landed a meeting with Huang was likely to walk away with funding. There were also worries about commitments to so-called neoclouds, such as CoreWeave or Nscale. These companies buy Nvidia GPUs, often with large amounts of debt, and rent the computing power to AI labs, startups, and enterprises. Nvidia has taken equity stakes in some of them and guarantees some of their data center leases. It has also agreed to rent back unused capacity at a fixed rate, which gives banks a floor that makes them more willing to lend. For example, Nvidia has agreed to buy up to $6.3 billion of CoreWeave’s unsold capacity through 2032. If Nvidia pulled back on some of these investments, the neoclouds most exposed would be those selling capacity to buyers without investment-grade credit, since they might not be able to finance GPUs without a backstop. This could have the knock-on effect of slowing some new data center projects. Huang’s personal touch extended to Nvidia’s supply chain, too. After his resignation, Elon Musk wrote on X that many of Nvidia’s critical deals were “a handshake with Jensen” and warned that “at least some of those critical deals will be lost” without him. With Huang back at the helm, investors expect Nvidia to keep acting as the AI industry’s lender; AI startups, labs, and neoclouds that lean on Nvidia for funding, compute, and credit backstops have more reason to expect those deals will keep coming at the pace they’d grown used to. The market seemed to agree, with Nvidia shares jumping more than 30% on Monday, and analysts at Melius Research and Bernstein quickly upgrading the stock. “Jensen Huang’s return is an enormous positive for Nvidia and the broader AI trade, removing a major source of uncertainty and restoring the visionary leadership that helped build the entire AI infrastructure ecosystem,” said David Miller, CIO at Catalyst Funds. “While questions remain about the ultimate returns on massive AI capital expenditures, today’s announcement meaningfully improves sentiment and reduces a major risk that had been hanging over the sector.”

sources.title: The 11 days that brought Jensen Huang back to Nvidia
sources.text: Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out founder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak. “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people,” Musk told the New York Times ‘ Andrew Ross Sorkin, appearing at the newspaper’s DealBook summit via videoconference while Musk was in China with President Trump. “He has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades. He understands the technology incredibly well.” Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return. “It is done,” he wrote. “The mistake has been corrected.” Musk’s reaction reflects the extraordinary political muscle that he and other powerful figures in Silicon Valley and Washington flexed to bring Huang back. The Nvidia board reinstated Huang as CEO , the company announced Monday. His ouster, initially triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, has gripped the business and political worlds for the past two weeks, and his return promises more shockwaves in the tech industry and the halls of power. Since Huang’s resignation was announced on Nov. 12, influential figures, from Musk to Trump , have waged a pressure campaign to make Huang CEO again, even as Nvidia’s board said it had moved on. Trump even called the board as it deliberated Huang’s reinstatement to push for his return. The reversal caps one of the most remarkable resurgences in business history, while raising numerous questions about how the company moves forward, given an internal investigation into Huang and a reported probe into Nvidia’s accounting by the Securities and Exchange Commission. This is a reconstruction of Huang’s ouster and return as it unfolded over a momentous 11-day period: On Oct. 29, the New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, was passing information to the Chinese government, and that she had a close relationship with Jensen Huang. The Times also reported that Trump was briefed roughly a year earlier but didn’t act. Subsequent reporting detailed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to gather intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO and possibly lobby for the sale of advanced chips to China. After the Times report, Huang told Bloomberg News there was nothing unusual about his relationship with Alice Huang, likening it to his dealings with Chinese customers and executives. “It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said. On Nov. 8, Huang publicly admitted to an affair, writing that “there is no excuse for what I did” and pledging to cooperate fully with Nvidia’s investigation, which the board announced the same day. The board, overseen by independent directors with outside counsel, said it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The next day, Chinese officials dismissed the spying claims as “pure fabrication out of thin air.” On Nov. 10, the independent directors hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation. The tech news website The Information reported that Alice Huang’s network had built companies to buy Nvidia chips, helping arrange about $7.5 billion in purchases, including of banned chips. The next day, the Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who has reported directly to him. Reached by phone, Huang told the Times , “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly” and hung up. Later that day, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s 10-member board was preparing to push Huang out and had called an emergency meeting. The alleged affair with Powell violated the company’s code of conduct, and Huang’s earlier assurances appeared to be false. By the next morning, Nvidia announced Huang had resigned . Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim CEO, and tech entrepreneur Harvey Jones was named Nvidia’s first board chair. The same day, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Richard E. Neal (D-Mass.) announced an inquiry into the administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify. Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second, unnamed Nvidia employee. It also reported that Huang misled Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Chief Marketing Officer Alison Wagonfeld in both fall 2025 and October 2026. Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14.35% in intraday trading, wiping out about $600 billion in value at the low, and ultimately closed down 4.34%. Almost as soon as Huang was ousted, a comeback effort took shape among tech and political elites and Nvidia’s own staff. A week ago, President Trump told reporters he would support reinstating Huang. “I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump said, adding that Huang had “learned a big lesson.” An Nvidia employee launched a website with an open letter demanding that the board reinstate Huang. As of Monday, more than 206,000 names appeared on the letter. Signatories included Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and tech investor Gavin Baker. The day after Huang resigned, Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner said in an open letter that Huang “has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known.” The same day, Nvidia’s board released a statement saying it was hiring an executive search firm and hadn’t yet approached any potential candidates. sources.title: What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia’s Colette Kress
sources.text: Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress led the company for 11 days during Jensen Huang's sudden but brief departure. When Nvidia's board officially reinstated Huang as CEO on Monday, the company also announced that Kress would continue in her role as CFO. The 59-year-old Kress currently has roughly 4.775 million shares directly and indirectly held, which makes her worth approximately $778 million at Monday's market close. The 63-year-old Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia stock soared 31% and the Nasdaq surged more than 6% Monday after the company announced that Huang would return as CEO, president and board director, effective immediately. Huang returned to the office Monday to crowds of Nvidia employees cheering his return . Kress, who stepped in as interim CEO during Nvidia's moment of crisis, joined the chipmaker as finance chief in September 2013 following stints at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments. As CFO, Kress oversees the balance sheet of a company aggressively financing many of the infrastructure deals that power the artificial intelligence buildout. Those agreements also raise concerns over circular financing and Nvidia's AI exposure in the event of a slowdown. In the first earnings call after Huang's resignation, Kress sought to reassure investors, raising the company's fiscal 2028 revenue-growth forecast to roughly 75% from 70%. She told analysts during a Q&A portion that it was "business as usual" at the company. She later told CNBC's Jim Cramer that customers have stood by the chipmaker and that demand continues increasing. "The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen, and that is our statement and what the board has decided to do," Kress said. During the company's first all-hands meeting after Huang's resignation, Kress also struck an optimistic tone , telling employees to "move forward" and mentioning pay raises. But Kress didn't manage to impress many market participants and insiders, who compared the interim chief to Huang. Last week, the stock recorded its worst week and longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis as AI stocks plummeted. "She just wasn't him," The Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman told CNBC. "I think she would have had to strengthen her bench around her a lot, because you have a visionary, product technology driven CEO that was literally the epicenter of the company. He was the entire identity." One person CNBC spoke with said Kress handled the situation with "skill and grace" while managing a tough job. The former Nvidia employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private, said Kress helped reassure the industry and that people should not be so "quick to rush to judgment." In the week since Huang's exit, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang belittled Kress, calling her "a deer in the headlights." Huang said in the press release announcing his return that he was "grateful" for Kress "leading NVIDIA during this period." "I think she is a fantastic CFO. I think Jensen probably has great confidence in her. I hope she stays," the former Nvidia employee said. "I don't think that she's going to be on thin ice when Jensen returns." Nvidia did not immediately respond to comment for this story.

sources.title: Six key questions raised by Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
sources.text: Jensen Huang made a dramatic return as Nvidia CEO on Monday, less than a week after board Chairman Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back. Nvidia shares surged as much as 36% during the session and closed 31% higher. The reversal followed a steep decline in Nvidia shares, which closed at $125.53 on Friday even after the company reported strong third-quarter results . A petition calling for Huang's return had drawn more than 200,000 signatures, according to its organizers. The rally spread across the broader market, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining 6.5% and the S&P 500 rising 4.7%, each posting its strongest session since April 2025. Nvidia's board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and that its investigation into Huang's conduct would continue. Still, the board's reversal, President Donald Trump's administration's role and continued scrutiny of Nvidia's China business leave major questions for both investors and lawmakers. Sen. Jack Reed, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Monday to appear before the committee to discuss the case. Reed did not lay out a specific list of questions for the two officials, but his statement cited reporting that Trump had been briefed by intelligence officials led by then-National Security Adviser Marco Rubio before intervening in support of Huang's return. Reed's call adds to mounting pressure on both Nvidia and the Trump administration to explain what they knew and when. Rep. Gabe Amo, D-R.I., vice ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang’s reinstatement could broaden congressional scrutiny rather than bring it to a close. “I think it frankly broadens the scope of the query,” Amo told CNBC, adding that lawmakers should also examine administration officials involved in decisions affecting Nvidia and chip sales to China. Amo said he expects the planned closed-door interview with Huang on Dec. 1 to proceed and that Congress would continue seeking answers both privately and publicly in the coming months. “He should start purchasing his plane tickets to Washington,” he said. “It is abundantly clear that this is ripe for questioning by Congress.” On Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, Jones said the board had accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Less than a week later, the board reversed course, saying Monday that it had unanimously voted to bring Huang back after discussions with him and input from senior U.S. government officials. Trump said he had spoken with board members and that his administration provided assurances based on the information available to it. But the board has not publicly detailed what it was told. Reed has called on Huang to disclose his communications with Trump and on Nvidia to release a transcript of the board's call with the president. Lawmakers are still seeking answers about the alleged smuggling of Nvidia products to China, their possible diversion for military use and possible advancement of Chinese AI capabilities. The Senate Banking Committee has scheduled Huang to testify on U.S. export controls on Dec. 3. House lawmakers have also confirmed closed-door interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2. "The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," Reps. John Moolenaar, Rick Crawford and Brian Mast said in a joint statement. Their inquiry may also examine what Nvidia knew about the customers and resellers involved, as well as what controls the company had in place. Other lawmakers have also sought to preserve the paper trail. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons had asked senior administration officials on Nov. 11 to retain records related to Nvidia exports of advanced AI chips to China and associated national security concerns. Nvidia has promised to hire a chief compliance officer and establish a committee overseeing national security and export controls. The board's investigation into Huang's conduct also remains underway. Josh Gilbert, eToro's lead analyst for APAC and the Middle East, said investors will be watching whether those new safeguards carry meaningful authority. Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said Nvidia has a limited window to prepare for the possibility that a future president may be less supportive of Huang. With Trump's term ending in two years, Luria argued that Nvidia needs a clearer plan for who could take over if Huang were forced to leave again. Gilbert pointed to Nvidia's roughly 75% revenue-growth forecast for the next financial year as evidence of strong near-term demand. The longer-term question, he said, is whether customer orders and artificial intelligence investment can sustain that pace. Luria told CNBC that concerns about the broader AI trade remain, including the cost of financing data centers, potential overbuilding by neocloud companies and obstacles to building new facilities. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said worries about whether AI spending is achievable and sustainable were not caused solely by Huang's departure. UBS, meanwhile, flagged Nvidia's roughly $390 billion in supply commitments and the need to keep demand flowing through its ecosystem. Gilbert said part of Monday's rally reflected investors recovering earlier losses rather than pricing in new growth. Bernstein restored its "Outperform" rating and kept its $200 price target, while UBS maintained its $220 target. "For the share price, it comes down to whether Nvidia can keep delivering as it has done over recent years," said Gilbert, adding that Huang's return could ease some concerns about Nvidia's longer-term outlook. sources.title: Trump endorses Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, says US has no evidence of wrongdoing
sources.text: President Trump praised Nvidia’s decision on Monday to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, saying on his social network Truth Social that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” The Nvidia board’s statement had also referred to consultations with “senior levels of the United States government” as informing its decision. It said that, based on that input, Mr. Huang’s reinstatement was deemed not a national security risk. In his comments on Monday, Trump claimed that U.S. Attorney General [Todd Blanche] had found no evidence that Mr. Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Notably, Attorney General Blanche has not yet made a formal statement on the case. There’s also indication that President Trump may have been aware of the decision before the announcement by the Nvidia board. Speaking to a PBS journalist over the weekend, he said of Huang “he’s back where he should be and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong.” Asked to clarify about whether he meant Huang would be reinstated, Trump said, “I hope so, I hope so.” Huang was accused of having multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a direct report at Nvidia and another unnamed employee. However, the affair of most concern was the one with the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation). Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions. Trump said last week that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below. The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. sources.title: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO — and we guess all other questions will be dealt with later
sources.text: In a stunning turnaround, Nvidia 's board has officially reinstated momentarily disgraced Jensen Huang as CEO. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," wrote the board in an official statement . The news comes after US President Donald Trump supported Huang's return, and US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent used some crafty wordplay to reverse his earlier comments that Nvidia needed to look "outside" for a new CEO. As he told CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday, "I said they need to go outside; Jensen is on the outside." Perhaps you've been fixated on tech outages (see Outlook, banks, FAA) or just preparing for and then playing GTA 6 for the last two weeks, and have no idea why Jensen Huang resigned from the chip company he co-founded 33 years ago. If so, here's the abridged version. Whispers about Jensen Huang's possible relationship with a Megapseed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), leaked a few weeks ago. The Singapore-based company is a big Nvidia customer. It may also allegedly be funneling Nvidia chips to China. With the exception of certain lower-powered chips, exporting US chips to China is against US policy. The FBI has been investigating whether Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy. As all this was coming to light, there were fresh allegations of Jensen Huang having affairs with multiple co-workers. Jensen Huang admitted in a memo to an infidelity and apologized, but with the new relationship revelations, he resigned. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. Almost as soon as Huang stepped down, there were calls for his return. He's been depicted as a unicorn founder and CEO : basically one of a kind and irreplaceable. Social media was split, or at least platforms were split. On Threads, the sentiment was generally anti-return, especially with a lack of clarity on what Huang and even the US government knew and didn't know about Alice Huang and Megaspeed. On X, there was a more full-throated call for his return. During Nvidia's November 17 earnings call, which was run by interim CEO Colette Kress, the board made it crystal clear that it was moving on, stating it "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." When it comes to business, the weight of opinion on social media carried about as much weight as a tinfoil feather. Pressure, though, from shareholders, and especially the White House, may have swayed the board. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government," revealed the board in its official statement. Jensen Huang does his best to sound contrite in the same Nvidia release: "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. " Trump has been unwavering in his support for Jensen Huang, and it's clear the President believes an Nvidia with Jensen Huang is more knowable than one with a new, potentially untested CEO. The President also quickly cheered Huang's return on Truth Social. Initially, it's business as usual for the world's most important AI company, but questions swirling around Jensen Huang, Alice Huang, Megaspeed, China, and the US officials will linger. To its credit, Nvidia is being somewhat transparent about this new reality, admitting that "Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," and its investigation of those events continues: "The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it." Still, this now seems like a largely toothless effort. As the board noted in its statement: "The Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk." That rapid reinstatement of Huang proves that whatever Huang did or didn't know, and what his interactions with Alice Huang may have enabled, doesn't really matter. Huang is back in the driver's seat without any answers. As these answers arrive, which might at least prove Alice Huang is a spy and that, thanks to her alleged efforts, China got Nvidia chips it should not have had access to, it's unlikely that the board will take any action. Jensen Huang's role as not only the leader of Nvidia, but now one of the world's most important and now untouchable AI executives, is likely cemented not just for the immediate future, but at least through the Trump administration's end. Two years from now, the world will have moved on; we'll have more agentic AI thanks to Nvidia's latest chips, maybe making decisions for us we no longer want to or feel qualified to handle. For example, getting to the root of what happened with Jensen Huang, Alice Huang, Megapseed, China, and the Trump Administration. It's also worth noting that, while the reinstatement of Jensen Huang may have helped Nvidia stock and the tech stock market at large, it will have zero impact on the price of technology running Nvidia GPUs. It's not like this choice was made to help consumers. This is a move intended to raise the fortunes of AI tech companies and AI development. Nvidia's old GPU/gaming business is likely immaterial, as is any whiff of clarity — and maybe justice — surrounding whatever did or did not happen with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. sources.title: Jim Cramer sees more upside for Nvidia stock with Jensen Huang back as CEO
sources.text: Nvidia's remarkable stock comeback isn't done yet now that Jensen Huang has returned as CEO , CNBC's Jim Cramer said Monday. "It's terrific to have this admittedly tarnished national treasure back leading Nvidia," the " Mad Money " host said. "It's kind of a miracle given the board's insistence that he would never get the CEO job again. But it's a miracle that saved the Nasdaq which, in turn, saved the market, at least for now." Nvidia shares soared 31.5% on the news, fueling a broader rally in AI infrastructure stocks. The S&P 500 jumped 4.7%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite surged 6.5%, with both indexes posting their best days since April 2025. Monday's rebound erased nearly all of Nvidia's decline following Huang's Nov. 12 resignation amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Before the rally Monday, the stock had fallen in all trading sessions since his departure. "Jensen's only one man, and Nvidia is only one company," he said. "But the truth is that Jensen is the linchpin that holds the AI solar system together, and Nvidia is the biggest beneficiary." Cramer argued that Huang's reinstatement removes a major source of uncertainty for investors, strengthening the case for a higher valuation. The chipmaker delivered blockbuster quarterly results last week, raising its revenue growth outlook to 75%, but the results did little to stem the sell-off as investors remained concerned about its leadership. "If it weren't for the Jensen overhang, and the insistence that Jensen could never come back, ... I think the stock would have been up significantly on that quarter," Cramer said. Still, Cramer cautioned that Huang's return doesn't erase the broader headwinds facing Nvidia. Growing political opposition to data center construction following the midterm elections could slow AI infrastructure expansion, while uncertainty surrounding chip sales to China threatens a potential source of demand. Meanwhile, a more hawkish Federal Reserve has pressured technology stock valuations as investors brace for higher interest rates. Those challenges, Cramer argued, make it difficult to justify a return to the $213 level Nvidia traded at before The New York Times first reported about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence on Oct. 29. But with Huang back at the helm and the company's growth outlook intact, he said the stock deserves a higher valuation. The stock currently trades at roughly 10 times earnings estimates for Nvidia's fiscal 2028, according to FactSet. "There is just no way that, with the return of Jensen, this stock deserves the same 10 times price to earnings multiple," Cramer said. "These things are subjective, of course, but to start, let's say this stock deserves to trade at twelve times next year's earnings estimate, which would make this a $199 stock," Cramer said. "That's my target." sources.title: A selloff, a POTUS, or a recession: What really made Nvidia bring Jensen Huang back as CEO?
sources.text: The instant the news hit the wires Monday morning that Jensen Huang was back in the job as Nvidia CEO, shares of the AI chipmaker surged 29% in premarket trading. They went on to notch their best session in more than 20 years, while the broad-market S&P 500 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq jumped about 4.7% and 6.5% respectively. What a change from last week, when the markets flashed red for two days and closed Friday in correction territory. The news, at least for Monday, appears to have revived the AI trade and helped erase more than a week’s worth of losses for both the equities market and the tech behemoth. Still, as investors celebrated and President Donald Trump took credit for Huang’s return, the big question looming over the stunning sequence of events revolved around cause and effect. Were the selloff and the Monday rally both reflections of Huang’s essential role in the global economy? Or was last week’s decline the result of broader, and still unresolved, instability in the markets that conveniently armed Huang’s supporters with a rationale to bring him back? The sudden change of mind within Nvidia’s board —insisting the former CEO had no future at the company last week, and then saying exactly the opposite on Monday—added to the questions and sense of intrigue. What led the company to change its mind so abruptly, and why now? Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, wasn’t surprised that the selloff might have pushed the board’s hand. “There is a good reason to think that, with shareholders in play, they would think maybe, ‘We need Jensen back just because the market is telling us so much now,’” he said . Tigay pointed to Nvidia’s blowout earnings report last week without Huang at the helm, adding that although the firm beat expectations, the stock still couldn’t catch a break. “The fundamentals of the stock were amazing, but the company is fundamentally different without Jensen. He is a visionary,” Tigay told Fortune. “He just has this longer-term view of where the technology is going and has been leading Nvidia correctly on that path for a long time. I think the stock market and shareholders wanted Nvidia with him and that vision.” (Equity Armor Investments, a wealth management firm, is an investor in Nvidia.) Governance experts shared similar sentiments. “The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia is clearly an attempt to restore market confidence and prevent further losses after Friday ended in correction territory,” Nick Reese, a professor at New York University’s School of Professional Studies Center for Global Affairs, told Fortune. That said, many of the long-standing causes of investor unease, particularly Nvidia’s role as the “central bank” financing a vast array of startups and potentially masking the true state of demand, have not gone away. If anything, Huang’s return could make the practice less likely to end (indeed, during Huang’s brief absence, Nvidia’s interim CEO had indicated a willingness to reassess some of the financing activities). And public backlash to building data centers, a key issue that helped Democrats sweep the recent U.S. midterm elections , is only likely to increase going forward—a significant headwind to the AI boom. For Huang’s supporters, including a very vocal cohort of tech founders and billionaires , the stock market selloff in recent days was proof positive of Huang’s importance and a warning sign of larger economic danger. “POTUS and JD’s intervention this weekend prevented a massive economic own goal this week for the US,” venture capital investor Chamath Palihapitiya posted on X on Monday. “They gave the Board what they needed to bring Jensen back.” Trump trumpeted his role, telling CNBC on Monday that he spoke with Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” and urged members to bring Huang back. “I convinced them,” Trump said. “I made the deal.” “People say, ‘Is it a threat to have him?’ No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump said of Huang. “I’m very, very happy that the company had the courage and the board had the courage to do the right thing, and they suffered for two weeks, and the company suffered greatly.” To be sure, Trump may have his own money in Nvidia. CNBC reported that investment accounts tied to the president have made 103 trades since he returned to the White House. Those transactions were worth a cumulative $27 million to $97.5 million. The White House says that Trump doesn’t control those trades, and that they are made by outside advisors. Washington could have something to lose without Huang as well: America’s position in the AI race. “I think that even the biggest China hawks thought, ‘Gosh, if this has reduced [Nvidia’s] market capitalization, and U.S. companies might pull back on their investments in AI … does this pose a threat to America leading in AI?’” said Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy. After all, there are several ways the U.S. could lose ground. Nvidia shed roughly $1 trillion in market value in the days after Huang resigned, and a long CEO search could have made companies think twice about funding the AI build-out that its chips power. Chinese customers might also move faster to domestic chips. And Washington would lose an executive who has spent years lobbying to sell American chips abroad. Finally, there are economic concerns. Without Huang at the helm, Moorhead said, “this could take us into a recession.” AI investment has become one of the main engines of U.S. growth, adding roughly 1.3 percentage points to real GDP growth over the past three quarters, Reuters reported Monday, citing Apollo Global’s data. If Nvidia’s slump scared companies into pulling back, the economy would lose a substantial source of expansion. But what’s next with Huang back on top? sources.text: After the leather-jacketed CEO, president, and co-founder of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, his company initially announced an investigation. However, after The New York Times reported there was evidence of another affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to him, a board meeting that night ended with Huang’s resignation , and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress was installed as the new interim CEO. In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies. Saying it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia’s board announced his return as CEO on November 23rd, less than two weeks after his resignation. Follow along below for all of the latest updates. After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO , following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened. Now, those of us who had some kind of basic education on what a “free market” is might find it objectionable to have the American president strong-arming a major American company. But our billionaire tech overlords care about the “free market” exactly as much as they care about “free speech,” which is to say not at all. Watching Silicon Valley cheer for what is, effectively, a sign of a command economy has certainly been bracing. But then, why would they give a shit? Their only real beliefs are that they should remain rich and above the law. Jensen may not have exchanged emails with Jeffrey Epstein, but he’s squarely at the Epstein table now. Trump did the TV circuit this morning to talk up how involved he was in Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday. He said on CNBC that he spoke to Nvidia’s board, adding, “I convinced them.” Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia’s office as CEO today to a crowd of applauding employees who stood and filmed the cofounder’s first moments back. “Thank you all for the second chances. I’m gonna be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang said, as shown in a video of his return. The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago cofounded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.” Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from The New York Times said he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency had enlisted that woman — Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was under investigation for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. It sure looked like President Donald Trump played a role in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO — and now the White House is making sure everyone knows he was. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, which was first reported by Semafor . “We have to protect our geniuses.” Trump later went on CNBC with a similar statement. “We have to protect our geniuses,” he said on the air. Trump said he “believed very strongly” that Huang should be reinstated. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did — I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents. But he did nothing wrong.” Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates , and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees , a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you. Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO. The company announced on Monday morning that the board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” In its statement, the board says that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump responded to the board’s decision in a post on Truth Social , saying Nvidia “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. sources.name: Xataka
sources.title: Jensen Huang menciona a su familia en sus primeras palabras tras volver a ser CEO de Nvidia
sources.text: Once días ha durado uno de los episodios más bizarros de la industria tecnológica reciente: el líder intocable de Nvidia fue destituido como CEO por varias relaciones extramatrimoniales, siendo la de Alice Huang la más espinosa por las sospechas de que podía ser una espía para China. Luego vino el caos bursátil y un trasfondo que deja claro lo mucho que depende Nvidia de Jensen. Tanto que hoy mismo se anuncia su regreso con plenos poderes . Vuelve como CEO, pero también como presidente y director de la junta de accionistas. Sus primeras palabras vienen en el mismo comunicado oficial del anuncio y que traducimos a continuación: Hay que leer estas palabras con lupa porque están escritas y medidas al milímetro . Cuando el cofundador de Nvidia habla de «humildad» y «compromiso renovado» y agradece la «deliberación» del consejo, está claro que lo que quiere es pedir una tregua pública tras once días de auténtico vértigo: desde su dimisión el pasado 12 de noviembre hasta el giro de 180 grados de una junta directiva que, apenas unos días antes, había descartado tajantemente su regreso. El subtexto es evidente: Huang asume de forma velada el desgaste reputacional de un escándalo personal que llegó a castigar la cotización de la compañía, pero al mismo tiempo vuelve desde una posición de fuerza tras quedar demostrado que ni los inversores, ni la plantilla, ni siquiera la Casa Blanca (no olvidemos el respaldo público de Donald Trump) concebían una Nvidia sin su arquitecto al timón. Esa misma lectura estratégica explica el reparto de agradecimientos con el que busca pasar página y blindar el futuro inmediato de la empresa . Al elogiar explícitamente el liderazgo de Harvey Jones al frente del consejo y el papel de Colette Kress como consejera delegada interina, Huang proyecta normalidad institucional y desactiva cualquier sospecha de fractura interna, justo mientras Nvidia mantiene abierta la investigación independiente y crea un nuevo puesto de director de cumplimiento normativo para disipar las dudas sobre seguridad nacional en Washington. Llama también la atención su mención expresa al apoyo de su familia , que funciona como una especie de cortafuegos para dar por zanjada la dimensión personal de la polémica (quizá como recordatorio a su yo del futuro), mientras que su apelación a liderar «una nueva revolución industrial» devuelve el foco al único terreno donde su figura resulta insustituible: el despliegue global de la infraestructura de inteligencia artificial, un argumento que Wall Street ha comprado de inmediato celebrando su vuelta con fuertes subidas antes de la apertura del mercado. En Xataka | Nvidia es el Super Glue de la industria de la IA. Sin Huang al frente, temen que sea pegamento de barra

sources.name: Computer Hoy
sources.title: Nvidia recupera a Jensen Huang como CEO tras semanas de incertidumbre y las acciones se disparan
sources.text: Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google. ¡Las acciones se disparan, Wall Street reacciona y persisten dudas sobre la compañía! Nvidia restituye a Jensen Huang como CEO tras once días de incertidumbre. Tras confesar la infidelidad junto al caso de espionaje y ser investigado por posibles filtraciones de secretos empresariales , Jensen Hueng fue revocado de su puesto y los nombres que sonaban con fuerza para el reemplazo eran Tim Cook o Eric Schmidt , pero eso parece que ya se terminó. A pesar de la crisis de liderazgo por la que ha estado pasando el exCEO de Nvidia durante las últimas semanas, las cosas están cambiando drásticamente porque el consejo de administración ha decidido restituir al cofundador de la gran compañía que lidera el mercado de las tarjetas gráficas con la RTX 5090 . La decisión parece llegar justo tras una fuerte presión política, dudas sobre el futuro de la marca y el impacto financiero que ha significado el cambio. Sí, el regreso de Jensen Huang está aquí , aunque el peso de su trabajo como jefe, después de los recientes inconvenientes, podría ser incluso más diferente de lo esperado. ¿ Quieres saber qué va a pasar con la próxima serie de las GPUs ? Puede que te interese todo lo relacionado con este caso porque también ha hecho que las acciones se disparen. ¿Huang está de regreso y Nvidia no requiere de otro CEO? ¿Qué está pasando con toda la compañía? Se desata una nueva oleada de noticias alrededor de este acontecimiento porque en un principio se pensaba que ya era más que evidente que ya no formaría parte del equipo después de estar por más de tres décadas. Pues bien, la junta directiva de Nvidia ha aprobado por unanimidad la restitución de Jensen Huang como director ejecutivo después de que la compañía asegurase haber consultado la decisión con "altos niveles" de la administración estadounidense. Tras ser categorizado como alguien sospechoso por ser infiel a su esposa con una espía china, la investigación ha dado como conclusión que la empresa considera que no existe un riesgo para la seguridad nacional que justifique apartar definitivamente a su fundador. Esto termina inclinando la balanza a favor de su regreso. Harvey Jones, presidente del consejo, defendió la decisión afirmando lo siguiente: Apenas se conoció la noticia, las acciones de Nvidia llegaron a dispararse más de un 30 % en las operaciones previas a la apertura de Wall Street. Según los datos difundidos tras el anuncio, la valoración bursátil de la compañía pasó de situarse ligeramente por encima de los 3 billones de dólares a superar los 4 billones en cuestión de minutos (aproximadamente 3,67 billones de euros), un salto que pone de manifiesto la enorme confianza que todavía genera el ejecutivo entre accionistas. El propio Huang no tardó en pronunciarse después de hacerse oficial su regreso. "No puedo esperar para volver al trabajo" , declaró el directivo. A la celebración también se sumó Donald Trump, quien defendió públicamente la reincorporación del empresario y aseguró que Estados Unidos necesita su liderazgo para mantener la competitividad tecnológica del país. La estrecha relación entre ambos había sido objeto de especulación durante los días previos, especialmente tras aparecer informaciones que vinculaban al fundador de Nvidia con varias investigaciones e interrogantes relacionados con operaciones comerciales internacionales, se indica en NVIDIA Newsroom . Aunque la restitución de Jensen Huang reduce la incertidumbre inmediata sobre el liderazgo de Nvidia, el movimiento está lejos de cerrar todas las preguntas que han surgido durante esta crisis . De hecho, la situación ha servido para mostrar hasta qué punto la compañía depende de su fundador. Diversas informaciones apuntan a que decenas de directivos reportan directamente al CEO y que Huang participa de forma activa en decisiones estratégicas que van desde acuerdos comerciales hasta inversiones y relaciones con clientes clave del negocio de la inteligencia artificial. Uno de los aspectos que más interés genera entre analistas e inversores es el denominado "círculo" financiero atribuido a Nvidia. El resultado era una red de operaciones que alimentaba la demanda de hardware. La entonces CEO interina y directora financiera, Colette Kress, habría planteado una revisión más estricta de estos mecanismos por considerar que algunos procesos necesitaban una mayor separación entre inversión estratégica y actividad comercial. Siguen existiendo dudas sobre determinadas operaciones internacionales relacionadas con el suministro de chips. Tampoco desaparecen los interrogantes sobre el modelo de crecimiento que ha impulsado a Nvidia hasta convertirse en una de las compañías más valiosas del planeta.

stories.summary: The states are seeking civil penalties and injunctions to stop Grok and X from creation and distribution of nonconsensual sexualized images.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims
sources.text: Lawsuits against Elon Musk's SpaceX are stacking up, with Virginia and Oregon becoming the first states to sue the company over issues with its Grok AI image generator. Versions of Grok and SpaceX's social network X have enabled users to generate and distribute explicit deepfakes based on real photos or videos of children and other people who did not consent, according to research by the Internet Watch Foundation , the Center for Countering Digital Hate and others. In separate complaints submitted to state courts as of Monday morning, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones argued that SpaceX failed to put safeguards in place to stop Grok and X users from making and sharing harmful deepfake images, especially alleged AI-generated child sexual abuse material. The complaints also allege that SpaceX has falsely represented its AI apps and social network (Grok and X) as generally safe, which the states see as a violation of Virginia's Consumer Protection Act or Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The matter is particularly concerning because X allows minors 13 and older to access its content. Rayfield and Jones both noted in their complaints that harms caused by non-consensual, sexualized images go beyond the victims depicted in the images. "This content can cause fear, distress, and anxiety in those who are unwillingly exposed to the content," Jones wrote. Rayfield wrote that such conduct "erodes important norms regarding consent and privacy and trivializes sexual imagery, abuse, and exploitation." In a statement emailed to CNBC by a spokesperson for SpaceXSI, and posted on the company's @Safety account on X, the company said, "When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement. Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors." At an NYC Council hearing in October , a SpaceX AI policy leader, Gabriela Castillo Madrid, said the company had appropriate "safeguards" and "strict controls" in place around its AI products. SpaceX was already facing multiple Grok- and X-related lawsuits, and government probes around the world, including by authorities in the U.K., Spain, Ireland, France and the state of California. In private-sector lawsuits filed against SpaceX in the U.S. concerning Grok and AI-generated, explicit images, litigation is still in early stages and is tracked by The Center for Internet Technology Addiction. When the city of Baltimore sued xAI, now owned and operated by SpaceX, the company argued that under Section 230, they were not liable for unwanted images. Section 230 is a federal law that largely shields online platforms from liability for users' content. SpaceX also sued a user in a federal court in the Northern District of Texas for breach of contract after he allegedly used Grok to create and distribute deepfake explicit images, including depictions of minors. Lawyers for Musk's company argued that Grok should be seen as "a neutral tool, subject to user control," and that any image generation "is the result of the user's prompts and directions." The new state suits add to legal pressure on SpaceX. Both Virginia and Oregon are seeking injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, while Virginia is also seeking restitution for consumers from Musk's company. Oregon submitted its complaint to the Multnomah County Circuit Court on Sunday evening, and Virginia submitted its complaint to the City of Richmond Circuit Court Monday morning . As of early Monday, the suits were pending the courts' acceptance. State attorneys general have recently succeeded in compelling U.S. social media companies to change their products and pay for alleged past harms. In August, for example, Meta settled a major federal case centered on allegations that the social media giant misrepresented the level of child mental health problems caused by its apps, Facebook and Instagram . Without admitting to wrongdoing, Meta agreed to pay states around $17 billion over a 10-year period and to make app changes that experts believe will help keep children safer online.

sources.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
sources.text: State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’﻿ State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’﻿ In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.” “Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement . “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.” The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos. In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX ) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift. In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors . xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios. Our testing at the Verge following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however. Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages. The X Safety team said in a statement released after the lawsuits were announced that it takes appropriate measures to address users who generate sexual content involving minors: “The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards. When some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year, we acted promptly to tighten its protections, which are designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people. To stay ahead of this disgusting and indefensible conduct, we keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics. We also implement sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt before an image is generated and check every output after.”

sources.text: Get more helpful Search responses by securely opting in to connect Google Wallet, Drive, and the Gemini app to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode. Your browser does not support the audio element. We’re adding Google Wallet and Drive to Personal Intelligence, allowing Search to provide answers based on your spending, documents, and chats. These updates help you manage finances, organize projects, and maintain context across your search threads. You can opt in to connect these apps by visiting your Search Personalization settings, where you remain in control of your data and can adjust your preferences at any time. Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, explains that you can now connect your apps like Google Wallet and Drive to Search for more personalized results. When you opt in, Search uses your own documents, spending habits, and recent activity to provide tailored answers. This helps you track financial goals, organize project information, and continue research tasks without repeating yourself. You remain in control and can manage these connections in your settings at any time. The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you. Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence — and we're introducing more personally relevant responses, so it's easier to find just what you need. Starting to roll out today, you can opt in to securely connect Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode , with support for Drive and the Gemini app following in the coming weeks — bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search. These apps join Gmail, Calendar, and Photos in delivering even more tailored responses with your personal context. To connect your apps to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, open Search Personalization, select Connected Apps, and then choose the apps you want to connect . You choose if and when you opt in, and you can turn those connections on or off at any time. You’re always in control of your personalization settings, and soon you’ll also be able to view the context AI Mode uses via the “Personalization” icon below any tailored response. If you want to edit anything simply let AI Mode know what to change, like responding in thread “I’m no longer a vegetarian.” You’ll also start seeing more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode, tailored to your recent search context. So if you’ve been researching and planning for a trip, you can pick up right where you left off in a new search thread without starting over or repeating yourself. You may opt out at any time.

sources.title: Google Search’s AI Mode can now tap into Drive and Wallet for more personalized responses
sources.text: Google announced on Monday that it’s expanding Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode with integrations for Google Drive, Google Wallet, and the Gemini app. Personal Intelligence is designed to offer users more personalized, context-aware answers by connecting to their Google apps and drawing on information from their digital lives. The feature can already connect to apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Photos. By bringing Personal Intelligence in AI Mode to Drive, Wallet, and the Gemini app, Google is leveraging the wealth of user data that’s already within its ecosystem. Since users rely on these services, the tech giant can deliver more personalized experiences that rivals aren’t able to match. Of course, not everyone wants AI looking at their Wallet and Drive, so connecting the apps is optional, and you can turn Personal Intelligence on or off at any time. Google says that connecting Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence lets users track their financial goals, cut everyday spending, and make better use of credit card rewards. The tech giant notes that if users choose to connect their Wallet, AI Mode can only read information from accounts and isn’t able to move or manage their money. As for Drive, the company says important information related to a project or major decision is often scattered across documents and spreadsheets. By connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence, AI can draw on those files to provide more relevant, personalized answers, such as creating a tailored plan for tax season. Users will also be able to share context between their Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, which means that if they explore an idea in the Gemini app, they won’t have to start over with AI Mode because it will already have the information, and vice versa. Additionally, Google says users will soon be able to view the context that AI Mode uses via a new “Personalization” icon that will appear below responses. The company also announced on Monday that users will start to see more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode that will be tailored to users’ recent search context. stories.title: Schumer puts Nvidia, Trump on notice after Huang reinstatement
stories.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that Congress is coming for answers — whether he's back at the top of the company or not. Why it matters: The embattled CEO's return to the board came as a shock to investors but sent Nvidia's stock through the roof . Now, some lawmakers are warning that his return raises national security concerns. What they're saying...

sources.title: Exclusive CNBC Transcript: See how Trump 'made the deal' to reinstate Huang as Nvidia CEO
sources.text: President Donald Trump said Monday that he personally intervened to secure Jensen Huang ’s return as Nvidia CEO, telling CNBC that he spoke with the chipmaker’s board before it reversed course and reinstated its co-founder. “I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC’s Eamon Javers during an interview on “Squawk on the Street.” Trump described his involvement in the decision, which came less than two weeks after Huang resigned, and addressed questions about national security concerns surrounding the Nvidia executive's return. Read the full transcript of Trump's interview with CNBC here.
